title: Postgres 19 is late because so many more bugs are being found now
titleZh: Postgres 19 is late because so many more bugs are being found now
author: soheilpro
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Over the past decade, the timing of PostgreSQL major releases has become very predictable: no earlier than the middle of September, and no later than the middle of October. This year is going to be different. PostgreSQL 19 most likely won’t be released until November, and it’s not impossible that the project could decide to postpone the release further.Moreover, this year, several rather large features were reverted quite late in the beta period: UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF, SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), and ALTER TABLE … MERGE PARTITION/SPLIT PARTITION were all reverted between August 27 and September 15. While major feature reverts are not especially uncommon immediately after feature freeze, which each year occurs on April 8, it is unusual to see multiple major features get pulled from the release at such a late date. So, what happened?The short answer is that LLMs happened. All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL’s code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There’s a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. That’s always been true, and it hasn’t stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What’s different now is that it’s become vastly easier to find those bugs. Fixing them has also gotten easier, but not to the same degree.Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL’s master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE. In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%.It’s possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but I don’t think anyone who works on the project really believes that’s the main cause. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years, but a lot more of the mistakes they made were quickly found by LLMs.And it isn’t just mistakes in the latest release. In the same time period, during 2025, there were 248 commits to REL_17_STABLE, and during 2026, there were 433 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In other words, the number of commits being back-patched not just to the release in progress but also to at least one prior release jumped by more than 74% in a single year. The reason for this is simply that a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very, very busy fixing them.And I think that’s also why we had so many late reverts, and why the release itself is delayed. Two factors are at play here.First, because so many more bugs are being found now, it takes more time to fix them. LLMs can draft fixes, but those fixes aren’t always correct or compliant with PostgreSQL standards. So, they still need to be reviewed and committed by humans, and those humans have not gotten any smarter between 2025 and 2026.Second, time that would have been spent reviewing what went into the release got diverted into addressing security issues and other bugs in the back-branches, and so it took longer to figure out what needed to be reverted before shipping v19.In the end, I don’t think that the delay in shipping PostgreSQL 19 is particularly concerning. It is not a long delay in the grand scheme of things, and it emerges directly from the project’s concern for quality.The long-term picture is less clear and in some ways more troubling: given that we have forty years of bugs that humans were unable to find but LLMs are quite capable of discovering, how are we ever going to catch up, and how will PostgreSQL continue to innovate? Right now, I’m not sure. What I do know is that I, and many others, are working really hard to figure it out.I became a PostgreSQL developer partly because the PostgreSQL code base is some of the cleanest and highest-quality code upon which I have ever had the privilege to work. The recent success of AI in finding bugs in that code base does not change my high estimation of it. It is not perfect – no software product is – but if it had more defects visible even to human eyes, the number of things found by LLMs would likely be even greater.There’s no escaping the fact that LLMs are going to require every PostgreSQL developer – and some extent, every software developer on earth – to raise their game. Every feature that we write from now until the end of our careers will be scrutinized by AI, and things that would have escaped forever unnoticed in an earlier era will now be found, perhaps in a matter of hours. That’s both a challenge and an opportunity.[This blog post originally appeared at https://neon.com/blog/postgres-19-is-late-and-its-ais-fault]

comments.author: BatteryMountain
comments.textRawHtml:
This is a good thing. Repaying technical debt is always a great thing.

On our own 1.5M loc system, we've found and fixed thousands of bugs, security holes and circular dependencies in the last year. Code quality has increased, test coverage increased. We've also recently set our compiler to treat warnings as errors, and to be as strict as possible. It is absolutely amazing to see the gaps being filled, it would've been an impossible task for human devs and IDE's would've made it very uncomfortable. We've also ironed out all the bugs and failure modes in our infrastructure automation / monitoring. Our next project is to eliminate all 3rd party dependencies, and after that to rebuild our frontends completely using zero frameworks, not touching npm ever again after that.

So when I read this about postgres, I was very happy that they found and pursued this side quest. They can make the codebase bullet proof.

children.author: Gigachad
children.textRawHtml: Avoiding 3rd party libraries seems like a false sense of security. You’ll stop seeing CVEs on the scanner reports, but the bugs are still there, just in your own code that is less well audited than public libraries.

children.author: BatteryMountain
children.textRawHtml:
I understand, but I would argue its better to have an in-house 1K lines of code that only does what we need and nothing else, it well tested and under our control, than to depend on some 50K lines of code (of which we might only use 10% of functionality and the others just getting in the way) that random's on the internet can modify, sometimes pulling in transient dependencies that we would really not have in a server environment, telemetry and other gremlins. It goes without saying that opensource packages will become even more juicy targets for malware/hackers to get into your systems like we've seen in the past month (and it will only become worse - you will be forced to pay technical debt or die).

The only "third-party" packages that we want to ideally allow/support would be provided from LTS versions of our runtime (in this case, packages provided by the dotnet team and audited by microsoft). So we will always try to build around what the framework provides. Second choice is our own code, third choice is open-source packages, fouth choice is a separate application/appliance (lets say ZenDesk for ticketing). Over time, we will reduce this footprint to only have dotnet team code and our own.

Remember most CVE's can be hidden on servers that are not publicly routable and don't have a real exploitation paths. The bits that are public (lets say a linux edge server with a web server on it, some firewalls, a couple of open ports) - these should be hardened to the max and not allow full access to all the services running behind it. We don't even give our internal services public IP addresses to make near impossible to route traffic to them.

Our git repo's are also not on public infrastructure (serious, think carefully about hosting on public services and if you really need it), never mind making the repo public.

We also have a dedicated secrets/certs manager, so no credentials are in codebases or pipelines. Very strict in this regard.

children.author: throw0101d
children.textRawHtml:
> Remember most CVE's can be hidden on servers that are not publicly routable and don't have a real exploitation paths.

The thinking of "it's inside so we're safe(r) from attacks" is a false sense of security, as (e.g.) Maersk learned with NotPetya:

* https://www.wired.com/story/notpetya-cyberattack-ukraine-rus...

* https://archive.is/Amlij

From the year 2000:

   NAT (particularly NAPT) actually has the potential to lower overall
   security because it creates the illusion of a security barrier, but
   does so without the managed intent of a firewall.  Appropriate
   security mechanisms are implemented in the end host, without reliance
   on assumptions about routing hacks, firewall filters, or missing NAT
   translations, which may change over time to enable a service to a
   neighboring host.  In general, defined security barriers assume that
   any threats are external, leading to practices that make internal
   breaches much easier.
* https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2993#section-9

children.author: kibwen
children.textRawHtml:
The purpose of the above comment is to highlight the flaw in the original premise. Surely we all agree that we would rather not be using a vibecoded cryptography library. But why is cryptography special? Why stop there? I would also rather not be using a vibecoded regex library, or a vibecoded codec parser, or a vibecoded web framework, etc.

The point being, if you weren't committed to maintaining your own implementation of a library before the advent of LLMs, having access to LLMs does not fundamentally change the calculus. The ability to generate code more quickly does not automatically grant an organization the capacity to maintain more code.
